title: Embedding Evaluation
scopeHtml: Scope: Measuring embedding quality for a specific use case: golden sets, recall@k, MTEB limits, domain eval.

notes.title: Why you must evaluate embeddings yourself
notes.html:
The idea. An embedding model turns text into a vector so that "similar meaning" becomes "close together". Whether a model does that well for your documents and your users' questions is an empirical question. Nobody can answer it for you, not the model vendor, not a leaderboard. Embedding evaluation is the practice of measuring, with numbers, how often your retrieval system finds the right content for the queries you actually care about. See also: the notes on embeddings (01_E1) for what a vector is and the short "Thresholds and evaluation" section there; this note goes much deeper into how to build the test, the maths, the code and the traps.

Why it exists. Teams pick an embedding model by reading a blog post or sorting a leaderboard, ship it, and then discover that the support bot misses "how do I get my money back" because the knowledge base says "refund policy". Without a measurement you cannot tell whether a new model, a new chunk size or a new index setting made things better or worse. Every change becomes an opinion. With a small test set, every change becomes a number you can compare in minutes.

Key terms (defined once).

  • Query: the text a user types or your system generates ("reset my password").
  • Corpus: all the documents or chunks you search over.
  • Relevant document: a chunk that a human agrees answers or supports the query.
  • Retrieval: given a query, return the top k chunks ranked by similarity.
  • Golden set (also gold set, ground truth, eval set): a fixed list of queries, each labelled with the chunks that are relevant to it.
  • Metric: a single number summarising how good the ranking is (recall@k, MRR, nDCG below).

What you are really measuring. Three separate things get mixed up:

  1. Embedding quality: does the model place relevant chunks near the query? (This note.)
  2. Index quality: does the approximate-nearest-neighbour index (HNSW, IVF) actually return the true nearest vectors? (Covered at the end; it is a different failure.)
  3. Answer quality: does the LLM write a good answer from the retrieved text? (Different evaluation; see the RAG notes.)

If the final chatbot answer is wrong, you need to know which of the three failed. Evaluating retrieval alone, before any LLM is involved, is cheap (no generation cost), fast (seconds) and deterministic.

Real products that do this. Search teams at every large company keep judged query sets (this is classical information retrieval practice going back to the TREC conferences in the 1990s). Vector database vendors (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant) and RAG frameworks (LlamaIndex, LangChain, Ragas) ship retrieval-evaluation helpers. The BEIR benchmark (2021) and MTEB (2022) are public collections of exactly this kind of test.

Real life. Buying running shoes. The shoe box says "best cushioning" (the leaderboard). You still try them on and run a lap (your own test), because your feet are not the average foot.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "we use the top model on MTEB" as the whole answer to "how did you choose an embedding model". Interviewers want to hear about your own golden set.
  • Confusing retrieval evaluation with end-to-end answer evaluation. Measure them separately.
  • Treating a vendor's "state of the art" claim as evidence for your domain.

notes.title: The evaluation loop step by step
notes.html:
The idea. Evaluation is a small loop you can run in a few minutes and repeat after every change. Here is the whole picture before we fill in the details.

 golden set                         corpus (chunks)
 (query, relevant ids)              (id, text)
        |                                 |
        |                          embed every chunk once
        |                                 v
        |                        vector matrix  [N x D]
        v                                 |
 embed each query  ---------------------> |
        |                                 v
        |                     score = cosine(query, every chunk)
        |                                 v
        |                       top-k chunk ids (ranked)
        +--------------> compare with relevant ids
                                          v
                          recall@k  MRR  nDCG@k  (one number each)

Step by step.

  1. Freeze the corpus. Pick a snapshot of chunks (with stable ids). If the corpus changes under you, scores move for reasons that have nothing to do with the model.
  2. Build the golden set (next section): query text plus the ids of the relevant chunks.
  3. Embed the corpus once with the candidate model. Remember the model's rules: query and document prefixes (for example some models need "query: " and "passage: " in front), maximum input length, and normalisation. Getting these wrong silently lowers every score, so a "bad" model result is sometimes your bug.
  4. Embed every query with the same model (using its query prefix if it has one).
  5. Score and rank. For a golden set of a few hundred queries and a corpus of up to a few hundred thousand chunks, brute force is fine: one matrix multiplication. Brute-force (also called exact or flat) search gives the true ranking, which is what you want when judging the model rather than the index.
  6. Compute metrics per query, then average.
  7. Record the result together with model_name, model_version, chunker_version, corpus_snapshot, date. A number without its recipe is useless a month later.
  8. Compare two candidates on the same golden set, and look at per-query wins and losses, not only the average.

Cost of one run. Embedding 100,000 chunks of 300 tokens is 30 million tokens (100,000 x 300 = 30,000,000). At a hypothetical 0.02 dollars per million tokens (verify current prices; it varies widely) that is 30 x 0.02 = 0.60 dollars. A local open model costs nothing but GPU time. The golden-set queries add a trivial amount. So comparing three models costs a few dollars, far cheaper than shipping the wrong one and re-embedding production later.

Production failure patterns.

  • Prefix mismatch: documents embedded without the prefix the model requires; recall drops 5 to 15 points with no error message.
  • Stale corpus snapshot: golden set ids point to chunks that were re-chunked and renumbered; every query then scores zero or, worse, a silently wrong match.
  • Eval run uses the ANN index, production uses another setting: numbers do not transfer.

Real life. A driving test: same route, same examiner rules, every time. If you change the route every time you cannot tell whether the driver improved.

Common interview traps.

  • Re-using the production vector index for model comparison. Each model needs its own index (vectors from different models are not comparable).
  • Forgetting to normalise vectors, then comparing raw dot products with cosine thresholds.
  • Reporting a metric with no k, no corpus size and no model version.

notes.title: Building a golden set
notes.html:
What it is. A golden set is a spreadsheet-sized file: each row is a real question plus the chunks that should come back. It is the most valuable artefact in the whole evaluation, more valuable than any metric code.

Why quality beats quantity. 150 to 300 carefully labelled, realistic queries beat 10,000 auto-generated ones. Start with about 100, grow over time.

Where queries come from (best first).

  1. Real user queries from search logs, support tickets, chat transcripts. Remove personal data first (names, emails, account numbers).
  2. Questions written by domain experts (a support agent, a lawyer, a doctor) who know how people actually ask.
  3. Synthetic queries generated by an LLM from your chunks (see the domain eval section). Good for scale, but they are easier than real ones because they copy words from the chunk.

How to label.

  • For each query, find the chunk(s) that contain the answer. Two reviewers independently, then resolve disagreements. Track inter-annotator agreement: if two humans disagree on 30 percent of labels, your metric is noisy no matter what the model does.
  • A useful trick for finding candidates: run two or three different retrievers (keyword BM25, two embedding models) and have the humans judge the union of their top 10. This avoids the trap where only the chunks your current system returns ever get labelled (pooling, the TREC technique).
  • Use graded relevance when helpful: 2 = directly answers, 1 = partially helps, 0 = not relevant. Binary labels (0/1) are simpler and fine to begin with.

What belongs in the set (the hard cases).

Case Example Why it matters
Paraphrase "get my money back" vs "refund policy" The core promise of embeddings
Exact identifier "error E4012" Embeddings often fail; keyword search wins
Acronym/jargon "PTO", "KYC" Domain vocabulary is rare in training data
Typos "pasword reset" Real users type badly
Multi-intent "cancel and get a refund" Two relevant chunks
Negation "can I NOT be charged" Embeddings are weak on negation
Unanswerable question about a product you do not sell Test that nothing high-scoring comes back (see thresholds in 01_E1)
Other language Hindi question, English docs Cross-lingual retrieval

A simple file format. JSON Lines, one object per line:

{"qid": "q17", "query": "how do I get my money back", "relevant": {"refund-policy-03": 2, "returns-faq-01": 1}, "tags": ["paraphrase", "billing"]}
{"qid": "q18", "query": "E4012", "relevant": {"errors-e4xxx-02": 2}, "tags": ["identifier"]}

Tags let you slice results later ("how are we doing on identifier queries?").

Hygiene.

  • Split into dev and test. Tune on the dev half; report the final number on the untouched test half. If you tune chunking and thresholds against all queries, your reported score is optimistic (overfitting to the eval set).
  • Version the file in git next to the code. Changing labels silently makes history incomparable.
  • Refresh quarterly from new production queries. A frozen golden set slowly stops resembling real traffic.

Production failure patterns.

  • Golden set written by the engineers who built the system uses the system's vocabulary, so scores look great and real users still fail.
  • Labels point to chunks by position ("chunk 7") instead of stable ids; re-chunking invalidates everything.
  • Only positive labels recorded: you cannot tell "no relevant chunk exists" from "we did not label it", so unanswerable queries are never tested.

Real life. A school exam. Questions written by the teacher only about what was taught in class will not reveal that students cannot handle questions phrased differently.

Common interview traps.

  • "Let the LLM label everything" without a human spot-check (typically sample 50 and measure agreement).
  • Evaluating on the same queries used to pick hyperparameters.
  • Ignoring unanswerable and ambiguous queries.

notes.title: Metrics explained with numbers
notes.html:
The idea. Retrieval returns a ranked list. A metric turns the list plus the labels into one number. We need a few because each answers a different question. Let k be the number of results you look at (commonly 5, 10 or 20, matching how many chunks your RAG prompt will contain).

Recall@k. Of the relevant chunks that exist for this query, what fraction appeared in the top k? recall@k = (relevant chunks in top k) / (total relevant chunks for the query). Averaged over queries. Some people use the looser hit rate@k (also success@k): 1 if at least one relevant chunk is in the top k, else 0. For RAG, recall@k is the key number, because if the answer chunk is not in the prompt the LLM cannot use it. Rule of thumb: pick k equal to the number of chunks you actually send to the model.

Precision@k. Of the k returned, what fraction are relevant? precision@k = (relevant in top k) / k. It tells you how much noise you stuff into the prompt. With k = 5 and 1 relevant chunk, the best possible precision is 0.2, so do not be alarmed by low precision when each query has only one correct chunk.

MRR (mean reciprocal rank). Look at the rank of the first relevant result; take 1/rank; average over queries. Rank 1 gives 1.0, rank 2 gives 0.5, rank 3 gives 0.333, not found gives 0. Worked example, three queries: first relevant at rank 1, rank 3, not in top 10. MRR = (1 + 1/3 + 0) / 3 = 1.333 / 3 = 0.444. Use it when only the top result matters (autocomplete, single-answer lookup).

nDCG@k (normalised discounted cumulative gain). Use it when relevance is graded and position matters smoothly.

  • Gain of a result = its relevance label (or 2^rel − 1 in one common variant).
  • Discount by position: divide by log2(position + 1). Position 1 has divisor 1, position 2 has 1.585, position 3 has 2, position 5 has 2.585.
  • DCG = sum of gain / discount over the top k.
  • IDCG = DCG of the perfect ordering. nDCG = DCG / IDCG, so it lies between 0 and 1.

Worked example (binary labels, k = 4). Two relevant chunks exist. The system returned relevance [0, 1, 0, 1] (positions 1 to 4).

  • DCG = 0/1 + 1/log2(3) + 0/log2(4) + 1/log2(5) = 0 + 1/1.585 + 0 + 1/2.322 = 0.631 + 0.431 = 1.062.
  • Ideal ordering [1, 1, 0, 0]: IDCG = 1/log2(2) + 1/log2(3) = 1 + 0.631 = 1.631.
  • nDCG@4 = 1.062 / 1.631 = 0.651.

Which to report. A good default trio: recall@k at your real k, MRR (did we put it near the top), nDCG@10 (to compare with published benchmarks, which use it). MTEB's headline retrieval score is nDCG@10.

The code (pure math, no library needed). The same function in three languages. Each takes the ranked list of returned ids and the set of relevant ids.

import math

def recall_at_k(ranked, relevant, k):
    return len(set(ranked[:k]) & set(relevant)) / len(relevant)

def reciprocal_rank(ranked, relevant):
    for i, doc in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
        if doc in relevant:
            return 1.0 / i
    return 0.0

def ndcg_at_k(ranked, rel_by_id, k):          # rel_by_id: {"doc": grade}
    dcg = sum(rel_by_id.get(d, 0) / math.log2(i + 1)
              for i, d in enumerate(ranked[:k], start=1))
    ideal = sorted(rel_by_id.values(), reverse=True)[:k]
    idcg = sum(g / math.log2(i + 1) for i, g in enumerate(ideal, start=1))
    return dcg / idcg if idcg else 0.0

# worked example from the text
print(ndcg_at_k(["n1", "r1", "n2", "r2"], {"r1": 1, "r2": 1}, 4))   # prints about 0.651
import kotlin.math.ln

fun log2(x: Double) = ln(x) / ln(2.0)

fun recallAtK(ranked: List<String>, relevant: Set<String>, k: Int): Double =
    ranked.take(k).toSet().intersect(relevant).size.toDouble() / relevant.size

fun reciprocalRank(ranked: List<String>, relevant: Set<String>): Double {
    val idx = ranked.indexOfFirst { it in relevant }
    return if (idx < 0) 0.0 else 1.0 / (idx + 1)
}

fun ndcgAtK(ranked: List<String>, relById: Map<String, Int>, k: Int): Double {
    val dcg = ranked.take(k).withIndex()
        .sumOf { (i, d) -> (relById[d] ?: 0) / log2(i + 2.0) }   // position = i+1, so log2(position+1) = log2(i+2)
    val idcg = relById.values.sortedDescending().take(k).withIndex()
        .sumOf { (i, g) -> g / log2(i + 2.0) }
    return if (idcg == 0.0) 0.0 else dcg / idcg
}

fun main() {
    println(ndcgAtK(listOf("n1", "r1", "n2", "r2"), mapOf("r1" to 1, "r2" to 1), 4)) // about 0.651
}
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class RetrievalMetrics {
    static double log2(double x) { return Math.log(x) / Math.log(2); }

    static double recallAtK(List<String> ranked, Set<String> relevant, int k) {
        Set<String> top = new HashSet<>(ranked.subList(0, Math.min(k, ranked.size())));
        top.retainAll(relevant);
        return (double) top.size() / relevant.size();
    }

    static double reciprocalRank(List<String> ranked, Set<String> relevant) {
        for (int i = 0; i < ranked.size(); i++)
            if (relevant.contains(ranked.get(i))) return 1.0 / (i + 1);
        return 0.0;
    }

    static double ndcgAtK(List<String> ranked, Map<String, Integer> relById, int k) {
        double dcg = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < Math.min(k, ranked.size()); i++)
            dcg += relById.getOrDefault(ranked.get(i), 0) / log2(i + 2.0);
        List<Integer> ideal = relById.values().stream()
            .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).limit(k).collect(Collectors.toList());
        double idcg = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < ideal.size(); i++) idcg += ideal.get(i) / log2(i + 2.0);
        return idcg == 0 ? 0 : dcg / idcg;
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(ndcgAtK(List.of("n1", "r1", "n2", "r2"),
            Map.of("r1", 1, "r2", 1), 4));   // about 0.651
    }
}

Production failure patterns.

  • Recall computed against an incomplete label set: unlabelled relevant chunks count as misses, so a better model that finds new relevant chunks is punished. Mitigate with pooled labelling and periodic re-judging.
  • Division by zero for queries with no relevant chunk (unanswerable). Handle them as a separate category, for example "fraction of unanswerable queries where top score is below threshold".
  • Averaging hides disasters: mean recall 0.90 can include a whole class of queries at 0.2. Always slice by tag.

Real life. Recall@k is "did the library's search page show the book on the first screen"; MRR is "how far did I scroll"; nDCG is "were the best books near the top, with a penalty for good books buried deep".

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up recall (how many of the relevant items were found) and precision (how many of the returned items are relevant).
  • Quoting nDCG without saying which k, and which gain formula (linear or 2^rel − 1).
  • Believing high MRR means high recall: MRR only looks at the first hit.
  • Forgetting that with one relevant chunk per query, recall@k equals hit rate@k.

notes.title: Running the harness and comparing models
notes.html:
The idea. Put the loop together: embed, rank, score, average. Brute force keeps the model comparison honest. Use a library (sentence-transformers in Python) or an API; keep the code small enough to run in a notebook or CI job.

Python (local open model, exact cosine search).

import json, numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer   # pip install sentence-transformers

def evaluate(model_name, corpus, golden, k=10, q_prefix="", d_prefix=""):
    model = SentenceTransformer(model_name)
    ids = list(corpus)                                    # corpus: {chunk_id: text}
    D = model.encode([d_prefix + corpus[i] for i in ids], normalize_embeddings=True)
    rec, rr = [], []
    for ex in golden:                                     # ex: {"query":..., "relevant": [ids]}
        q = model.encode([q_prefix + ex["query"]], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
        order = np.argsort(-(D @ q))[:k]                  # cosine == dot for unit vectors
        ranked = [ids[j] for j in order]
        rel = set(ex["relevant"])
        rec.append(len(rel & set(ranked)) / len(rel))
        rr.append(next((1 / (n + 1) for n, d in enumerate(ranked) if d in rel), 0.0))
    return {"model": model_name, "recall@k": float(np.mean(rec)), "mrr": float(np.mean(rr))}

# print(evaluate("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5", corpus, golden))   # verify the model id and its prefix rules

Kotlin (backend, using any embedding function you supply). Java and Kotlin usually call an embedding API or a LangChain4j EmbeddingModel; the evaluation maths is plain arithmetic.

data class Example(val query: String, val relevant: Set<String>)

fun dot(a: FloatArray, b: FloatArray): Float {
    var s = 0f; for (i in a.indices) s += a[i] * b[i]; return s
}

// embed: your own function (e.g. a LangChain4j EmbeddingModel or an HTTP call). Vectors must be unit length.
fun evaluate(
    corpus: Map<String, String>, golden: List<Example>, k: Int,
    embed: (String) -> FloatArray,
): Pair<Double, Double> {
    val docVecs = corpus.mapValues { embed(it.value) }
    var rec = 0.0; var mrr = 0.0
    for (ex in golden) {
        val q = embed(ex.query)
        val ranked = docVecs.entries.sortedByDescending { dot(q, it.value) }.take(k).map { it.key }
        rec += ranked.toSet().intersect(ex.relevant).size.toDouble() / ex.relevant.size
        val idx = ranked.indexOfFirst { it in ex.relevant }
        mrr += if (idx < 0) 0.0 else 1.0 / (idx + 1)
    }
    return rec / golden.size to mrr / golden.size      // (recall@k, MRR)
}

Java (same idea).

import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class EvalHarness {
    record Example(String query, Set<String> relevant) {}

    static float dot(float[] a, float[] b) {
        float s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) s += a[i] * b[i]; return s;
    }

    // embed: your own function (LangChain4j EmbeddingModel or an HTTP client); vectors must be unit length.
    static double[] evaluate(Map<String, String> corpus, List<Example> golden, int k,
                             Function<String, float[]> embed) {
        Map<String, float[]> docs = new HashMap<>();
        corpus.forEach((id, text) -> docs.put(id, embed.apply(text)));
        double rec = 0, mrr = 0;
        for (Example ex : golden) {
            float[] q = embed.apply(ex.query());
            List<String> ranked = docs.entrySet().stream()
                .sorted((x, y) -> Float.compare(dot(q, y.getValue()), dot(q, x.getValue())))
                .limit(k).map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();
            Set<String> hit = new HashSet<>(ranked); hit.retainAll(ex.relevant());
            rec += (double) hit.size() / ex.relevant().size();
            for (int i = 0; i < ranked.size(); i++)
                if (ex.relevant().contains(ranked.get(i))) { mrr += 1.0 / (i + 1); break; }
        }
        return new double[] { rec / golden.size(), mrr / golden.size() };   // {recall@k, MRR}
    }
}

The Kotlin and Java versions are brute force and fine for thousands of chunks. Above roughly 100,000 chunks, do the evaluation in Python with numpy (one matrix multiplication) or use FAISS (IndexFlatIP, exact inner product), which is the pragmatic route even for a Java shop since evaluation is offline.

Reading the result. An example output table (illustrative numbers):

model            dim   recall@10   MRR    nDCG@10   cost to embed corpus
small-open-384   384     0.78      0.52    0.61      free (CPU, 20 min)
mid-open-768     768     0.84      0.58    0.67      free (GPU, 5 min)
api-large-3072  3072     0.88      0.63    0.72      about 6 dollars

The last model is better, but it also costs 8x the storage of the first (3072 / 384 = 8). Whether +10 recall points justify 8x storage and a vendor dependency is a product decision, and now you can make it with data.

Everything that must be held equal when comparing models: same corpus snapshot, same golden set, same chunking, same k, same normalisation, each model's required prefixes and truncation length.

Production failure patterns.

  • Silent truncation: model A truncates at 512 tokens, model B at 8192; with long chunks B "wins" because it reads more text, not because it is smarter. Report chunk length alongside the score.
  • Different tokenizers inflate cost comparisons: price per token is not price per document. Compute total tokens per model.
  • API non-determinism / version change: the same API model name may be updated; log the version and re-run the baseline before concluding anything.

Real life. A bake-off between three caterers: same menu, same guests, same judges, and you also write down the price per plate.

Common interview traps.

  • Using dot without normalising and calling it cosine.
  • Comparing a model that sees 512 tokens with one that sees 8192 and attributing the difference to quality.
  • Choosing purely on the score without computing storage (vectors x dimensions x 4 bytes) and latency.

notes.title: MTEB: what it is and where it misleads
notes.html:
What it is. MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, Muennighoff et al., 2022) is a public suite that runs an embedding model on many datasets across task types: retrieval, classification, clustering, semantic textual similarity (STS), pair classification, reranking and summarisation. Each task type has its own metric (for example nDCG@10 for retrieval, V-measure for clustering, Spearman correlation for STS). Models are ranked on a public leaderboard (hosted on Hugging Face). Multilingual and domain-specific variants exist (for example MMTEB and language-specific versions; verify current names). The retrieval part builds on BEIR (2021), a set of retrieval datasets that includes MS MARCO, Natural Questions, FiQA (finance), SciFact and TREC-COVID.

Why it exists. Before MTEB, each paper evaluated on a different handful of tasks, and models looked excellent where they were measured and unknown elsewhere. MTEB gave one common yardstick, which is genuinely useful as a shortlist generator.

Where it misleads (know these cold).

  1. Average hides the task you care about. The leaderboard default sorts by an average across dozens of datasets, mixing classification and clustering that you may never use. Look only at the retrieval column, and better still only at datasets resembling yours.
  2. Your data is not their data. Public datasets are Wikipedia, web questions, forum posts, some scientific text. If your corpus is legal contracts, Kotlin crash logs, product SKUs, Hindi-English mixed chat, or medical notes, the ranking can reorder. A model 3 points ahead on average can be behind on your domain.
  3. Test-set contamination and overfitting. The test sets are public and the training sets of many models include similar or identical data. Some leaderboard entries are tuned for MTEB. The leaderboard has introduced flags for models with possible training-data overlap (verify the current state). A rising score may reflect memorisation rather than better generalisation.
  4. Short, clean inputs. Many benchmark documents are short and clean. Real corpora have long PDFs, tables, boilerplate, OCR errors and code. Context length behaviour (8192-token models) is barely tested.
  5. Score differences are often within noise. Gaps of 0.5 to 1 nDCG points between neighbours are frequently not meaningful (see the statistics section). Leaderboard rank 4 versus rank 9 is rarely a real difference.
  6. No cost dimension. The raw leaderboard ranks quality only. A model that is 1 point better but 10x larger, 4x slower and 8x more storage may be the wrong choice. (The leaderboard shows model size and embedding dimensions; use them.)
  7. Queries unlike yours. BEIR queries are often keyword-ish or single questions; real users write long, messy, multi-part questions, and RAG systems also generate queries with an LLM.
  8. Static snapshot of a moving target. Model ranks change monthly; mark any leaderboard claim "verify".

How to use MTEB properly (a three-step recipe).

  1. Filter to the task type (retrieval) and your language(s), and to models you can host or afford.
  2. Take the top 3 to 5 plus one small cheap baseline and one BM25 baseline (keyword search is a strong baseline; embeddings do not always beat it, especially on exact identifiers and rare terms).
  3. Run your golden set on the shortlist. The result of step 3 decides.

How to run MTEB yourself. The mteb Python package can run chosen tasks on your model (verify the current API in the docs; it changes). It is also the right tool when you train a model and want public numbers. For choosing a model, your own set matters more.

Production failure patterns.

  • A team switches to the current leaderboard leader, recall on their internal tickets falls 6 points, because the leader was trained on web-style Q and A and the tickets are terse log lines.
  • The leader needs 4096 dimensions; the vector store bill rises 4x (4096 / 1024) against the previous model.

Real life. A university ranking: useful for building a shortlist, useless for deciding whether a specific department will teach you what you need.

Common interview traps.

  • "MTEB average is the best predictor of my use case": no, retrieval subset plus your own data is.
  • Not knowing that the main retrieval metric is nDCG@10.
  • Not mentioning contamination and the cost dimension (size, dimensions, latency).
  • Mixing up MTEB (embedding models) with leaderboards for chat models.

notes.title: Domain evaluation with synthetic queries and hard negatives
notes.html:
The idea. A real golden set is slow to build. A hybrid approach: use an LLM to generate queries from your own chunks, and use embeddings plus an LLM judge to find hard negatives, chunks that look relevant but are not. Then a human reviews a sample. This gives you hundreds or thousands of in-domain test cases in an afternoon. It extends your real set; it does not replace it.

Step by step.

  1. Sample N chunks from the corpus (cover every product area; stratify, do not sample only the biggest document).
  2. For each chunk ask an LLM: "write 2 questions a user would ask that this passage answers; do not copy phrases from the passage; vary the style (short, long, keyword-only)."
  3. Label (query, source chunk) as relevant.
  4. Filter bad queries: the check "retrieve with BM25 and see if the source chunk comes back at rank 1" finds queries that are too easy (copying words); the check "does another chunk also answer it" finds ambiguous queries (the source chunk is not the only correct one).
  5. Human-review a random 10 percent; if more than about 15 to 20 percent are bad, change the prompt and regenerate.
  6. Mine hard negatives: for each query take high-scoring chunks that are not labelled relevant; ask a judge (human or LLM) whether they actually answer it. Those that do not are hard negatives (used to stress-test the model and, later, to fine-tune it); those that do are missing positives you must add to the labels.

Code: generate synthetic queries with the Anthropic API. Model id from the project defaults (verify before relying on it); key from the environment.

import anthropic, json

client = anthropic.Anthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

def make_queries(chunk_text, n=2):
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-5-5",       # verify model id in the docs
        max_tokens=300,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"Write {n} different questions a customer might ask that the passage below answers. "
            "Do not reuse phrases from the passage. Vary length and style. "
            "Return only a JSON list of strings.\n\nPASSAGE:\n" + chunk_text}],
    )
    return json.loads(msg.content[0].text)   # production: validate and retry on bad JSON

# print(make_queries("Refunds are issued to the original payment method within 5 business days."))

Slicing results for domain insight. The overall number is least useful. Break down by tag and look at the worst slices:

slice               n    recall@10   note
paraphrase         120     0.91
identifier (E4012)  40     0.45      embeddings miss exact tokens -> add BM25 (hybrid)
negation            25     0.52      "not refundable" matches "refundable"
hindi query         60     0.70      multilingual model needed?
long multi-intent   35     0.58      split query, or retrieve per sub-question

Each weak slice maps to a fix: hybrid search (BM25 + vectors fused with reciprocal rank fusion), a reranker (a cross-encoder that rescores the top 50 to 100 for a precision boost), query rewriting, a different model, or fine-tuning.

Fine-tuning as the end of the road. If a domain slice stays weak, you can fine-tune an open embedding model with (query, positive chunk, hard negative) triples using a contrastive loss (for example via sentence-transformers with MultipleNegativesRankingLoss; verify the current API). Typical gains on narrow domains with a few thousand good pairs can be large, but you must keep a held-out test set that was never used in training, and you must re-embed the whole corpus afterwards. Only do this once evaluation shows a gap that simpler fixes did not close.

Production failure patterns.

  • Circular evaluation: queries generated by the same model that is then evaluated (or by a model whose style the embedder was trained on) look unrealistically easy. Use a different generator or mix in real queries.
  • Leakage: synthetic queries copy rare words from the chunk, so even BM25 scores 95 percent and the benchmark cannot separate models.
  • Duplicated chunks in the corpus: the "wrong" duplicate is returned, labelled a miss; deduplicate or label all copies as relevant.
  • LLM judge drift: using an LLM to judge relevance with a changing prompt or model changes labels; pin and version it.

Real life. A flight simulator: you generate many scenarios cheaply, but you still do check flights with a real instructor.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming synthetic data fully replaces real queries.
  • Forgetting hard negatives, which are what separate good models from average ones.
  • Not mentioning hybrid search or rerankers as the cheaper fix for identifier and precision problems.
  • Fine-tuning before measuring (and without a held-out set).

notes.title: Statistics: is the difference real?
notes.html:
The idea. A golden set is a sample of possible queries. If model A scores recall@10 of 0.84 and model B 0.86 on 200 queries, B might just have been lucky. You need a feel for noise before you celebrate.

Confidence interval for a proportion. For a hit-rate style metric with proportion p over n queries, the standard error is sqrt(p(1 - p) / n). With p = 0.80 and n = 200: SE = sqrt(0.8 x 0.2 / 200) = sqrt(0.0008) = 0.0283. A 95 percent interval is roughly p ± 1.96 x SE = 0.80 ± 0.055, i.e. 0.745 to 0.855. So a 2-point gap on 200 queries is well inside the noise. With n = 1000: SE = sqrt(0.16 / 1000) = 0.0126, interval ± 0.025. Four times the data halves the interval width (width shrinks with the square root of n).

Paired comparison is much sharper. Both models see the same queries, so compare per query: count queries where only A hits (a), only B hits (b), both or neither (ignored). If a and b are close, there is no difference; use a sign test or McNemar's test (on a and b only) or a paired bootstrap (resample queries with replacement 1000 times, compute the metric difference each time, take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles). If the interval of the difference excludes 0, the gap is probably real.

import numpy as np

def paired_bootstrap(scores_a, scores_b, iters=2000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    d = np.asarray(scores_b) - np.asarray(scores_a)         # per-query differences
    boots = [rng.choice(d, size=len(d), replace=True).mean() for _ in range(iters)]
    return float(d.mean()), np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])   # (mean diff, 95% interval)
import kotlin.random.Random

fun pairedBootstrap(a: DoubleArray, b: DoubleArray, iters: Int = 2000): Triple<Double, Double, Double> {
    val d = DoubleArray(a.size) { b[it] - a[it] }            // per-query differences
    val rnd = Random(0)
    val means = DoubleArray(iters) { d.indices.map { d[rnd.nextInt(d.size)] }.average() }.sortedArray()
    return Triple(d.average(), means[(iters * 0.025).toInt()], means[(iters * 0.975).toInt()])
}
import java.util.*;

public class Bootstrap {
    static double[] paired(double[] a, double[] b, int iters) {
        int n = a.length; double[] d = new double[n]; double mean = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { d[i] = b[i] - a[i]; mean += d[i] / n; }
        Random rnd = new Random(0); double[] boots = new double[iters];
        for (int t = 0; t < iters; t++) {
            double s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += d[rnd.nextInt(n)];
            boots[t] = s / n;
        }
        Arrays.sort(boots);
        return new double[] { mean, boots[(int) (iters * 0.025)], boots[(int) (iters * 0.975)] }; // mean diff, low, high
    }
}

Practical rules.

  • Fewer than about 100 queries: treat results as a smoke test only.
  • Decide the metric and the "good enough" margin before looking at results (for example "switch only if recall@10 improves by at least 3 points with a CI above zero").
  • Do not test twenty variants and report the best one: with many comparisons some win by chance (multiple comparisons). Confirm the winner on the untouched test split.

Index-level recall is a separate number. Production uses approximate search (HNSW, IVF; see 01_E1). Measure ANN recall@k: for a sample of queries, compare the ANN top-k with the exact brute-force top-k: ann_recall = |ANN ∩ exact| / k. A typical target is 0.95 to 0.99, tuned with efSearch (HNSW) or nprobe (IVF). A low retrieval score with a high ANN recall means the model is the problem; a good offline score that does not appear in production often means the index parameters or a metadata filter (post-filtering returns fewer than k) are the cause.

Production failure patterns.

  • Shipping a "+1.5 point" change that was noise, then being unable to reproduce it.
  • Evaluating exact search offline but running a poorly tuned ANN index in production.
  • Reporting the best of many runs.

Real life. Judging two basketball players from five free throws each: you cannot tell. Watch fifty each, and have them shoot the same shots.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring a winner from a 1 to 2 point gap on a small set.
  • Using unpaired comparison when the queries are shared.
  • Mixing up embedding quality and ANN recall.
  • Peeking at the test split during tuning.

notes.title: Production monitoring and common failures
notes.html:
The idea. The offline golden set tells you how the system was. Production traffic changes, and embedding systems degrade silently: no exception is thrown, answers just get worse. Evaluation therefore continues after launch.

What to monitor.

  1. Regression test in CI: on every change to chunking, embedding model, prefixes, preprocessing or index settings, run the golden set (a few minutes) and fail the build if recall@k drops by more than a set margin. This is the highest-value habit in the whole note.
  2. Probe queries on a schedule: a frozen set of 50 to 100 queries run daily against the live system; alert if recall or the average top-1 similarity moves. This catches an embedding vendor silently updating a model.
  3. Online signals: thumbs up or down, "no results" rate, share of queries whose best score is below your threshold, rate of users rephrasing the same question within a minute (a strong sign retrieval failed), click-through on cited sources.
  4. Fresh failures into the golden set: every reported bad answer becomes a new labelled test (after you find the relevant chunk). The set then grows from reality.
  5. Index health: ANN recall sample (above), p95 latency, filter selectivity.

Typical production failures and how evaluation exposes them.

Symptom Likely cause How the eval finds it
Quality dropped after a deploy Chunker or cleaning change CI golden-set regression
Gradual decline Corpus or query drift Daily probe set, rising "no good match" rate
Sudden drop, code unchanged Provider updated model version Probe set; compare against logged model version
Good for English, bad for Hindi Weak multilingual coverage Slice by language tag
Exact codes never found Dense-only retrieval Slice "identifier"; add BM25 hybrid
Fine offline, poor online ANN under-tuned, filters, truncation Compare ANN recall vs exact; test with real filters
New product line unanswered Corpus not re-embedded or new vocabulary Tag by product; add labelled queries

Re-evaluation triggers (re-run the full comparison when): the model or version changes, chunk size changes, a new language or domain is added, the corpus grows by an order of magnitude, or the vector DB or quantisation changes (for example moving from float32 to int8 or binary quantisation; measure the recall loss, typically small for int8 and larger for binary, verify on your data, often recovered by rescoring top candidates with full vectors).

Cost and latency in the decision. Quality is one axis. Also tabulate: dimensions (storage = vectors x dims x bytes: 10 million vectors x 1024 dims x 4 bytes = 40.96 billion bytes, about 41 GB, before index overhead), embedding latency per query (affects p95 for the whole chatbot), maximum input length, license, and whether the vendor can deprecate the model (re-embedding cost). Some models support Matryoshka training, letting you truncate vectors to fewer dimensions; evaluate the truncated size on your golden set (for example 1024 down to 256 would cut storage by 4x) rather than assuming it is free.

A minimal CI check in the three languages. Fail the build when recall drops against a saved baseline.

def test_retrieval_regression():
    baseline = json.load(open("eval/baseline.json"))["recall@10"]      # saved from last good run
    result = evaluate("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5", corpus, golden, k=10)  # function from the harness section
    assert result["recall@k"] >= baseline - 0.02, f"recall fell: {result['recall@k']:.3f} vs {baseline:.3f}"
// JUnit 5 style; evaluate() is the harness function from earlier, embed is your embedding client.
@org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
fun retrievalDoesNotRegress() {
    val baseline = 0.84                         // load from a checked-in baseline file in real code
    val (recall, _) = evaluate(corpus, golden, 10, ::embed)
    org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertTrue(recall >= baseline - 0.02, "recall fell to $recall")
}
// JUnit 5; EvalHarness.evaluate is the harness function from earlier.
@org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
void retrievalDoesNotRegress() {
    double baseline = 0.84;                     // load from a checked-in baseline file in real code
    double recall = EvalHarness.evaluate(corpus, golden, 10, this::embed)[0];
    org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertTrue(recall >= baseline - 0.02, "recall fell to " + recall);
}

Real life. A smoke alarm test on the first of every month: the house may look fine, but you want to know the alarm still works before the fire.

Common interview traps.

  • No regression test: the typical story of a "harmless" chunking tweak that cost 10 points unnoticed.
  • Looking only at average top-1 similarity as a quality metric: it measures confidence, not correctness.
  • Forgetting vendor-side model updates as a cause of silent drift.
  • Ignoring the cost axes (storage, latency, re-embedding) in the final model choice.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
One paragraph. Embedding evaluation means measuring, on your own labelled queries, how well a model plus your chunking and index return the right chunks. Build a golden set (real queries, hard cases, stable ids, dev and test split), score with recall@k (matched to the k you send to the LLM), MRR and nDCG@10 using exact brute-force search, and compare models paired on the same set while holding corpus, chunking, prefixes and truncation constant. Use MTEB only to shortlist, because averages hide your task, public data is not your domain, and contamination and noise are real. Extend a small human set with LLM-generated queries and hard negatives, slice results by tag to find weak spots, and fix them with hybrid search, rerankers or fine-tuning. Check that gaps exceed noise using confidence intervals or a paired bootstrap, separate model quality from ANN index recall, and keep a regression test and probe set running in production.

Key points to remember.

  • Evaluate retrieval separately from generation; recall@k is the gate for RAG.
  • Formulas: recall@k = found relevant / all relevant; MRR = mean of 1/rank of first hit; nDCG = DCG / ideal DCG with discount 1/log2(position + 1).
  • Worked values: MRR of ranks 1, 3, miss = 0.444; the nDCG@4 example = 0.651.
  • 150 to 300 realistic labelled queries beat thousands of synthetic ones; include typos, identifiers, negation, unanswerable and other-language cases.
  • MTEB (headline retrieval metric nDCG@10) is a shortlist tool, not a decision; always run your own set. Leaderboard facts: verify.
  • A 2-point gap on 200 queries is inside the roughly ±5.5 point 95 percent interval; use paired comparison.
  • ANN recall (index) and embedding quality (model) are different failures.
  • Log model name, version, chunker version, corpus snapshot with every result; re-run on any change; keep a CI regression test.

Likely interview questions. How would you choose an embedding model for a legal-search product? (shortlist from MTEB retrieval and language, build golden set with experts, compare recall@k and cost, hybrid with BM25, test noise.) Why did recall drop after a deploy and how would you find out? (CI regression, versions, prefixes, chunker.) Why is MTEB not enough? (average, domain gap, contamination, no cost, noise.) How many queries do you need? (hundreds; confidence interval maths; paired tests.)
